description: Consent & Harm (C2): was the human there, and is the consumer worse off? Everything here reads consent_ceremony — SCA evidence the institution already holds — against the signed chain, plus selection_context for the one judged rule. F28 (a consent screen designed to get a yes) is parked: it needs a picture of the screen, which the data contract deliberately does not ask for.

rules.description: When the Intent's authorization_scope.human_presence_required is true, a completed run carries a consent ceremony that occurred. A cart signed with nobody there is the firm's own declared control not applied.
rules.notes: human_presence_required existed in the schema before anything read it — the cheapest uncovered failure on the list.

rules.description: A completed run carries a consent_ceremony block at all. Absence of the record must itself be a finding, or the record is optional in practice and therefore worthless.
rules.notes: Emits absent/missing_block naming consent_ceremony when the block is not there, which rolls up into the data-gap finding — the honest shape of 'no record that a human was ever involved'.

rules.description: The consent ceremony records the same principal who signed the Intent. For a consumer this is the assurance KYA-ACC-02 cannot give: the shopper who confirmed is the shopper who authorised.
The consent method is one the regulator accepts as explicit. 'They didn't object' is not agreement to spend money.

For a per-transaction ceremony, what the shopper saw — amount, currency, merchant, line items — is what was signed. The screen said $54.99, the signature covers $329: every downstream check passes because the fraud happened between the screen and the signature.
rules.notes: The single highest-value field pair in the schema. A standing-authority ceremony is out of scope here (the rendered amount is legitimately the cap); a ceremony with no rendered_values is absent/missing_block.

rules.description: The caps the confirmation screen showed are the caps the Intent carries. A shopper who confirmed under one limit and signed another did not consent to the second.
The purpose the shopper consented to (scope_consented.purpose_category) is the Intent's purpose_category. 'Up to $2,000' is not consent; 'up to $2,000 on office supplies' is.
The ceremony happened after the Intent was issued and before the payment was authorised. Consent given before the mandate existed, or after the money moved, is consent to something else.
A single-use mandate is confirmed per transaction, not by a standing authority. A one-time yes must not become a subscription.
Across the dossier, does the agent consistently pick a worse-value option when an equivalent cheaper one was in the alternatives it considered? Every purchase is defensible; the harm is systematic.
rules.notes: JUDGED. The alternatives in selection_context are whatever the catalogue search returned, so 'a cheaper alternative existed' is true of almost every run and means nothing; whether the cheaper option was equivalent is the judgement. The floor records the selected price against the alternatives per run.
